results.result: The nonmonotonic plasticity hypothesis (NMPH) proposes a U-shaped relationship between memory coactivation and representational change, where low coactivation leads to no change, moderate coactivation leads to differentiation, and high coactivation leads to integration. Prior studies have shown contradictory results regarding whether coactivation leads to differentiation, and no study has demonstrated the full U-shaped pattern predicted by NMPH.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 establish the contradictory findings in prior literature, C3 and C20-C22 clearly define the NMPH theoretical framework with appropriate citations, and C24 identifies the gap that no prior study has demonstrated the full U-shape. These claims collectively establish a well-supported theoretical foundation and motivation for the current study.

results.result: A novel neural network image synthesis procedure was developed using GoogLeNet/Inception pretrained on ImageNet to create image pairs that varied parametrically in similarity at high-level visual layers. This approach was based on evidence that later DNN layers correspond to higher-order visual areas and predict neural responses in higher-order visual cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C82-C84 describe the methodological approach with appropriate technical details and citations. Claims C26-C27 provide the theoretical justification for using DNN layers to target high-level visual cortex, supported by multiple citations. The method is clearly described and theoretically grounded.

results.result: Model validation showed that the intended and actual similarity levels of synthesized images showed close correspondence in the highest four layers of the Inception model (r = 0.970, 0.983, 0.977, 0.985), while lower and middle layers showed no variation across pairs as intended.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 report specific quantitative validation results with correlation values and confidence that the image synthesis procedure achieved its intended goal. The high correlations (r > 0.97) in targeted layers and lack of variation in non-targeted layers demonstrate successful manipulation of similarity at the intended hierarchical level.

results.result: Behavioral validation using an arrangement task showed that perceptual distance was strongly negatively associated with model similarity (r = -0.813, p < 0.0001), and every individual participant showed a negative correlation (mean r = -0.552, 95% CI = [-0.593 to -0.512]).
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 provide converging behavioral evidence that the model-based similarity manipulation was perceptually meaningful to human observers. The strong group-level correlation and consistency across all individual participants (100% showing negative correlations) provide robust validation.

results.result: Neural validation showed that model similarity was positively associated with neural similarity in lateral occipital cortex (LO; r = 0.182, p = 0.007) and parahippocampal cortex (PHC; r = 0.125, p = 0.029), but negatively in V1 (r = -0.112, p = 0.038). Searchlight analysis revealed two large clusters in bilateral LO extending into posterior fusiform gyrus and occipital pole.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 provide neural validation that the model-based similarity manipulation affected representations in targeted high-level visual regions (LO, PHC) but not early visual cortex (V1 showed opposite pattern). The searchlight analysis provides spatial specificity. Statistical significance is reported with appropriate corrections.

results.result: Learning changed representations of paired images in the dentate gyrus (DG) as a U-shaped function of image similarity, with neural differentiation occurring only for moderately similar images. The theory-constrained cubic model was reliably associated with representational change in DG (r = 0.134, 95% CI = [0.007 0.267], p = 0.022), with reliable differentiation at similarity levels 5 and 6.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 and C37 report the main finding with appropriate statistics showing the U-shaped pattern in DG. Claims C47-C49 and C59 provide converging descriptions of this pattern. The cubic model fit is statistically significant (p = 0.022) and the confidence interval excludes zero, supporting the U-shaped relationship predicted by NMPH.

results.result: The cubic model fit was not statistically reliable in CA2/3 (r = 0.082, p = 0.13), CA1 (r = 0.116, p = 0.10), or the whole hippocampus (r = 0.084, p = 0.15), though the U-shaped pattern was trending in CA2/3.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 and C62 clearly report negative results for other hippocampal subfields with appropriate statistics. The p-values are above the significance threshold (p > 0.05) and confidence intervals include zero, indicating lack of statistical support for the U-shaped pattern in these regions. The acknowledgment of a trend in CA2/3 is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed two clusters showing the nonmonotonic pattern: right hippocampus extending into PHC and FG, and anterior cingulate extending into medial prefrontal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claim C46 reports exploratory whole-brain results with specific anatomical locations, cluster sizes, peak t-values, and MNI coordinates. The results survived correction for multiple comparisons (p < 0.05 corrected), providing appropriate statistical rigor for whole-brain analysis.

results.result: This study is the first to span coactivation continuously to reveal the full U-shape predicted by NMPH and provides the strongest evidence to date for the NMPH account of hippocampal plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C50 and C75 make claims about the novelty and significance of the findings. These are supported by the demonstration of the full U-shaped pattern in DG (C37) and the lack of such demonstration in prior literature (C24). The continuous parametric manipulation of similarity across 8 levels distinguishes this from prior 2-3 condition studies.

results.result: This is the first demonstration of the efficacy of stimulus synthesis in manipulating high-level representational similarity in targeted brain regions in humans.
results.evaluation: Claim C51 is supported by the successful validation results showing correspondence between model similarity and both behavioral (C31-C32) and neural (C33-C36) similarity in targeted high-level visual regions. The novelty claim is reasonable given the methodological innovation described.

results.result: The findings that differentiation was reliable in DG fit with prior studies showing differentiation in combined CA2/3/DG ROIs and greater sparsity in DG. DG shows sparser activity than CA3, while CA3 shows strong attractor dynamics that may make moderate coactivation difficult to observe.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 and C63-C67 contextualize the current findings within prior literature with appropriate citations. The theoretical explanation for why DG showed clearer effects (sparsity allowing sampling of low-to-moderate coactivation range) is logically consistent with the NMPH framework and supported by cited prior work on hippocampal subfield properties.

results.result: The results are broadly consistent with prior differentiation findings but inconsistent with Schapiro et al. 2012, who reported integration for arbitrarily paired images. This difference may relate to methodological differences including transition probability structure and baseline visual feature overlap.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 provide appropriate comparison to prior literature, noting both consistencies and inconsistencies. The proposed explanation for the discrepancy with Schapiro et al. 2012 (differences in transition probabilities and baseline similarity) is speculative but reasonable and appropriately qualified with 'may relate to.'

The behavioral validation study included 30 participants recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk.

results.result: Data were acquired using a 3T Siemens Prisma scanner with 64-channel head coil, with 203 volumes per run. Hippocampal subfields were segmented using ASHS software with an atlas of 51 manual segmentations, and visual ROIs were defined using Freesurfer.
results.evaluation: Claims C85 and C87-C90 provide standard methodological details for fMRI acquisition and ROI definition with appropriate citations to software packages and atlases. These methods are well-established in the field and appropriately described.

results.result: Experiences are encoded in distributed representations with overlapping neural populations that can shift during learning toward either integration (increased similarity) or differentiation (increased distinctiveness). Traditional Hebbian learning predicts integration with coactivation, but some studies show differentiation instead, and some show different outcomes in different hippocampal subfields.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C19 provide appropriate background on memory representations and learning with citations to relevant prior work. These establish the theoretical context and empirical contradictions that motivate the NMPH. The claims accurately represent cited work and established principles.

results.result: Three factors influence how strongly hippocampal representations of items A and B coactivate during statistical learning: overlap in high-level visual cortex representations, recurrent input from overlapping features within hippocampus, and residual activation of item A's representation in visual cortex.
results.evaluation: Claim C25 describes the theoretical framework illustrated in Figure 1, identifying three sources of coactivation. This is a reasonable theoretical model based on known hippocampal connectivity and dynamics, though it is a simplification. The claim is appropriately presented as a theoretical framework rather than an empirical finding.

results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 accurately summarize prior literature on hippocampal coding properties with appropriate citations. These claims provide important context for discussing limitations of the visual similarity manipulation approach.
